title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
This is the opposite problem, where the same kind of observation is split across many files, for example one file per year or one file per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them together with bind_rows(), or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule. Each kind of observational unit gets its own table, and the tables are linked together by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake, but realistic, patient records that are stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients as CSV files, and in the HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data usually doesn’t come to us as a folder of CSV files. It’s stored and shared using data standards.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, where data like a patient, an encounter, or an observation is sent as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on databases from many hospitals

All of these follow the same idea as the paper’s third rule, with one table (or resource) for each kind of observational unit, linked together by IDs.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data. A good plot answers that question clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer, one at a time, with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

Regression, when the outcome is quantitative. What will this house sell for? How heavy will this baby be at birth?
Classification, when the outcome is categorical. Will this patient’s cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we’ll fit a linear regression. On Wednesday we’ll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

text:
Models need tidy data
A model formula like price ~ sqft expects the data to have one row per observation (each house sale) and one column per variable (the price and the size), which is exactly what tidy data gives us.

title: From tidy data to models
section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Fit it with tidymodels

house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)

title: Tidy data
text:
What is tidy data?


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value



Rules from R for Data Science (2e), chapter 5. Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst, from the Openscapes blog (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
The original definition (2014)
The original Tidy Data paper from 2014 defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

The third rule is really about databases, where data is split into separate tables and joined back together. The newer definition replaces it with “each value is a cell”. We’ll come back to observational units at the end, in the optional Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
The Tidy Data paper lists five common ways data gets messy:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which are in the optional Observational units section.

text:
Tidy the weeks

billboard_tidy <- billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE # drop weeks the song was not on the chart
  ) |>
  # the date at a rank = the date it entered + (week - 1) weeks
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)

title: Tidy data
text:
Pivot longer, then wider

weather_tidy <- weather |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("d"),
    names_to = "day",
    names_prefix = "d",
    names_transform = list(day = as.integer),
    values_to = "temp",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = element, # tmax and tmin become their own columns
    values_from = temp
  ) |>
  select(id, date, tmax, tmin) |>
  arrange(id, date)

Function

Doing many steps at once
We can save each step as its own object,

penguins_3 <- select(penguins_2, species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)

penguins_nested <- select(
  filter(mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000), flipper_len > 190),
  species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg
)

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data. A good plot answers that question clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer, one at a time, with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
This is the opposite problem, where the same kind of observation is split across many files, for example one file per year or one file per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them together with bind_rows(), or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule. Each kind of observational unit gets its own table, and the tables are linked together by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake, but realistic, patient records that are stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients as CSV files, and in the HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data usually doesn’t come to us as a folder of CSV files. It’s stored and shared using data standards.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, where data like a patient, an encounter, or an observation is sent as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on databases from many hospitals

All of these follow the same idea as the paper’s third rule, with one table (or resource) for each kind of observational unit, linked together by IDs.

What is tidy data?

The original definition (2014)
The original Tidy Data paper from 2014 defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

The third rule is really about databases, where data is split into separate tables and joined back together. The newer definition replaces it with “each value is a cell”. We’ll come back to observational units at the end, in the optional Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
The Tidy Data paper lists five common ways data gets messy:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which are in the optional Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Problem 1: column headers are values
This is a Pew survey that counts people by religion and income. The income brackets are column headers, but they’re really values of an income variable.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

Regression, when the outcome is quantitative. What will this house sell for? How heavy will this baby be at birth?
Classification, when the outcome is categorical. Will this patient’s cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we’ll fit a linear regression. On Wednesday we’ll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Models need tidy data
A model formula like price ~ sqft expects the data to have one row per observation (each house sale) and one column per variable (the price and the size), which is exactly what tidy data gives us.

title: From tidy data to models
section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Fit it with tidymodels

house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)

title: From tidy data to models
text:
More than one predictor
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_m X_m
\]
To use more predictors, we add them to the formula.

recipe(price ~ sqft + beds + baths, data = Sacramento)

Now each slope is how much the outcome changes for one predictor, when the other predictors stay the same.
